= Repeated Glasgow Marriages, 1400 – Present =

This page is part of the '''Glasgow One‑Name Study'''.  It analyses two profile‑sets drawn from the project’s working spreadsheets (‘‘File 1’’ = 1400‑1800; ‘‘File 2’’ = 1400‑Present) to show how often the Glasgow surname allied with the same circle of families—and why those alliances mattered.

* ‘‘File 1’’ – 809 profiles, 41 repeat pairings (up to 1800)  
* ‘‘File 2’’ – 3 545 profiles, 1 201 repeat pairings (1400‑present)  

Records where '''LNAB = Current''' or either surname was ‘‘Unknown’’ were excluded.  Spelling variants (e.g. ‘‘Nicol’’ ≈ ‘‘Nichol’’) were merged when their Levenshtein similarity was ≥ 0.85.

== Family Backgrounds: Major Glasgow Marriage Connections (1400‑Present) ==
The summaries below explain who these families were, why the Glasgow clan married them repeatedly, and how those connections shaped migration, land‑holding, and religious life.

; '''Cunningham'''  
Prominent Lowland lineage centred on Kilmaurs (Ayrshire); chiefs were Earls of Glencairn and patrons of the Protestant Reformation.  Cunninghams were also ‘‘undertakers’’ in the Ulster Plantation, receiving 5 000 acres in Donegal.  Multiple Glasgow–Cunningham unions therefore linked the Glasgow name to noble rank **and** to Ulster land.

; '''Finley / Finlay'''  
Ancient Gaelic name (*Fionn‑lagh*, “fair warrior”).  After the clan’s eclipse near Inverness, many Finleys joined the Scots‑Presbyterian community in Ulster; their descendants included Rev. Samuel Finley, President of Princeton.  Glasgow–Finley marriages tightened a transatlantic ministerial network that spanned Highlands → Ulster → Colonial America.

; '''Anderson'''  
A pan‑Scottish patronymic—Lowland burgesses and Highland septs alike.  Glasgow merchants named Anderson sat on the burgh council by 1650, and Andersons were ubiquitous among Ulster‑Scots settlers.  Repeated intermarriage wove the Glasgow family into that burgess‑diaspora web.

; '''Wilson'''  
One of Scotland’s top three surnames by 1800.  Wilsons appear as ship‑masters, coopers, and elders on both banks of the Clyde.  Matrimonial links gave the Glasgows a ready‑made network across every parish register and Presbyterian session book in the west.

; '''Smith'''  
Scotland’s commonest name.  Early Glasgow–Smith marriages often joined artisan dynasties in the Clyde Iron Works district, anchoring the family in urban craft guilds.

; '''Robertson'''  
Highland chiefs of Struan (Clan Donnachaidh) and numerous Lowland burgesses.  Ties to Robertsons supplied Gaelic prestige plus trading cousins from Perthshire to Ulster.

; '''Stewart'''  
Cadet branches of the royal house settled around Renfrewshire and the Lennox; Stewarts were also major ‘‘undertakers’’ in Ulster.  Glasgow–Stewart marriages thus conferred both aristocratic cachet and Irish plantation opportunities.

; '''Davidson'''  
A Clan Chattan sept whose tacksmen held Breadalbane lands; later successful merchants.  Marrying Davidsons linked the Glasgow line to Highland heritage and north‑country patronage.

; '''Glenn / Glen'''  
Locative surname found on both sides of the North Channel.  Glasgow–Glenn unions bridged Clyde shipping interests with Ulster Presbyterian communities.

; '''Weir'''  
Norman‑derived Weirs of Blackwood (Lanarkshire gentry) plus occupational ‘‘weir‑keepers.’’  Ties to Weirs consolidated property along the Middle Clyde and added a whisper of Norman glamour.

== Significance of the Pattern == of the Pattern ==
{| cellpadding="6" style="border:1px solid #aaa; background:#f9f9f9"
| '''Social Cohesion''' || Repeated alliances cemented a dense web of god‑parents, kirk elders, and trading partners, giving the extended Glasgow kindred a reputational safety‑net in every parish record from Ayr to Ulster.
|-
| '''Economic Power''' || Dowries, liferents, and merchant partnerships kept land and capital “in the family.” By 1750 the Glasgow‑Cunningham‑Anderson circle controlled contiguous properties from Kilmaurs to Glasgow Cross and ran export houses on the Clyde.
|-
| '''Political Reach''' || Allied cousins sat as provosts in Glasgow, undertakers in Ulster, militia colonels in Virginia, and even as presidents of Princeton.  Kin marriage multiplied the clan’s influence across three kingdoms and two continents.
|-
| '''Migration Chains''' || The same surnames recur in passenger lists: Cunninghams, Stewarts, Wilsons, Pattons, Campbells.  Glasgow relatives were thus greeted by cousins at every way‑station from Derry to Pittsburgh.
|-
| '''Religious Leadership''' || Presbyterian ministry flourished in the network—Finley, Henry, and Anderson kinsmen filled pulpits from Ayrshire to Pennsylvania, giving the clan moral authority and educational leverage (e.g. Rev. Samuel Finley, President of the College of New Jersey).
|}

== Modern‑Period Leader Families (brief profiles) ==
* '''Henry''' – Ulster sept Ó hInneirghe plus Lowland Hendrys; supplied kirk elders and schoolmasters across Ulster and the Ohio Valley.
* '''Bell''' – Border riding clan pacified by relocation to Ulster; later pillars of frontier Presbyterian communities in America.
* '''Patton''' – Border variant of Patrick; Colonel James Patton’s Shenandoah settlement illustrates the family’s pioneer drive.
* '''Campbell''' – Argyll magnates whose cadets flooded Glasgow; by 1841 Campbell was the city’s commonest surname, giving the Glasgow clan cousins in every municipal office.
